Chapter 4: Naming the Pattern—The Power of Language and Recognition
Have you ever felt that sense of relief when you finally find the right word to describe something you’ve dealt with for years? For a lot of people, the term “mansplaining” brought that exact relief. Suddenly, there was a way to talk about that all-too-familiar experience—being talked down to, corrected, or brushed aside by someone who just assumes they know better. The word itself might be new, but let’s be real—the feeling it captures? That’s been around forever.
Before “mansplaining” entered our vocabulary, it was tough to put your finger on what was happening. Sure, there was that mix of irritation, disbelief, maybe even helplessness—but what was really behind it? Was it just rudeness? A clash of personalities? Or was there something deeper at play? Without a name, the pattern stayed hidden, easy to ignore, and even easier to dismiss as random, one-off moments.
But then—once “mansplaining” caught on—everything shifted. Suddenly, people could call out a specific behavior, name it for what it was, and push back. The act of naming made what was once invisible, impossible to miss. Private frustration turned into public conversation. And just like that, it became obvious: this isn’t about one person’s bad habit. It’s a reflection of bigger power dynamics—of how we listen, who we trust, and whose voices get heard.
Here’s something to really pay attention to: language isn’t just about describing what happens to us. It actually shapes how we see ourselves, and how we see each other. When you name a behavior, you make it possible to spot it, challenge it, and even imagine a different way forward. “Mansplaining” isn’t just a label—it’s a tool. A way to say, “Hey, this isn’t okay.” And sometimes, that’s the first step toward real change.
Of course, not everyone welcomes this shift. Some people bristle at the word, maybe write it off as an overreaction, or say it unfairly targets men. Others argue, “Hey, not every guy does this,” or, “Women can be condescending too.” But here’s the thing—this isn’t about pointing fingers at individuals. It’s about shining a light on a bigger pattern—a habit of assuming authority, of speaking over someone, of dismissing expertise just because of gender.
Naming a pattern like this does more than change one conversation. It opens up space for people to reflect and start questioning the assumptions we’ve carried for years. You start to notice the little ways women’s voices get sidelined—not just in everyday chats, but in big decisions, in leadership, in public life. Naming the problem is the start—it’s how we begin to shake up the status quo and imagine something better.
Let me share a story that really brings this idea to life. Picture a woman who’s used to being interrupted in meetings. After she hears the term “mansplaining,” she starts paying attention. She keeps a tally of every time she’s talked over or corrected. The list grows fast, and so does her awareness. She decides to share what she’s noticed with her colleagues, and suddenly, there’s a real conversation about how to make things more inclusive. That simple act of naming the problem? It actually leads to change—new policies, a more mindful culture, and people being more thoughtful about how they interact.
And it’s not just about this one word. Throughout history, whenever people have pushed for justice, they’ve relied on the power to name injustice—to give a voice to things that once felt unspeakable. As our world keeps changing, new words and ideas keep popping up, helping us recognize and resist old patterns of power.
At its heart, naming is about recognition. It’s about really seeing what’s happening—and being seen yourself. It’s how we push back on the way things have always been and say, “Everyone’s voice matters here.” The hope? With each new word, each honest conversation, we edge closer to a world that’s fairer, more equal, and just a little more open to real change.
